Profulla Kumar Chakraborty -------- Appellate.
Vs. 
Anil Proshad Choudhury and others -------- Respondents.
full_judgment: 5. All that is needed is to see whether on the facts found by the trial Court the tenant appellant can get any reversal of the decision of the Courts below. It is to be observed that the learned Judges of the High Court Division has only considered one aspect of the finding of the trial Court, that the tenant paid rent for four months in a lump for Agrahayan, Pous, Magh and Falgoon, 1375 B.S. and got a receipt for three months whereas he could not produce rent receipt for the month of Falgoon, and it has been observed that payment of rent in lump does not help the tenant from the mischief of default. The proposition in our opinion though correct has been stated in a sweeping manner which requires to be modified in the light of the decision given in Runyan Ali's case by this Division. A tenant by making payment of rent in limp of rent in terms of section 18 (1) and 18 (5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, unless there is a contract to the contrary or such payment is covered by waiver and acquiescence on the part of the landlord. However, this is a question of fact which is to be established in each particular case by the tenant desiring to raise this as a special plea in his defence. The grievance of the tenant was that he paid rent in lump for four months, he got receipt for three months and he did not get receipt for the fourth month. He did not raise any plea of waiver on the contrary; he raised the plea of habitual payment of rent in lump which he failed to establish before the trial Court. So, his payment of rent in lump does not save him from the mischief of the Rent Control Ordinance making him a defaulter. Apart from this, it is to be observed that from Falgoon, 1375 B.S. to the filing of the suit, the tenant attempted to deposit rent with the Rent Controller, but it appears that he had deposited rent once for three months at a time by Ext, A, covering Chaitra, Baishakh and Jaistha, and then again for two months by Ext.A (3) covering Bhadra and Aswin. These payments of rent clearly are not in compliance with section 19 of the Ordinance and come within the rule of default as set out in Ramjan Ali's case. Looked at from any standpoint, the defence of the tenant appellant does not stand.
